text: That morning, riders appear out of the steam. They are [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) warriors. And behind them, crossing the world's first national park, are as many as eight hundred men, women and children, with nearly two thousand horses, running from the United States Army.

This is Henrys Lake, in Idaho, just west of the park. On August twentieth, some thirty miles west of here, [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) warriors raided the Army's camp at night and ran off most of its mules. The general in charge, Oliver Otis Howard, stopped here for days to rest and resupply his men.
Within days, by about August twenty-third, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) entered Yellowstone, near where the West Entrance is today.
They followed the Madison and Firehole rivers upstream, into the Lower Geyser Basin. And that's where they ran into the tourists.

The tourists were a party of nine, most of them from [Radersburg](/ɹˈeɪdɚzbɝɡ/), Montana. Among them were George Cowan, his young wife Emma, and Emma's brother and sister, Frank and Ida Carpenter. They had come to see the geysers.

Meanwhile, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) held a council about the captives. On August twenty-fifth, near Mud Volcano, they let Emma, Ida and Frank go free. Poker Joe himself rode with them back across the river, and pointed them toward safety.
Earlier that same day, the whole [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) caravan had crossed the Yellowstone River at a shallow place near Mud Volcano. Today, it's called [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) Ford.

Not every encounter went the way of the Cowans'. On August twenty-sixth, near Otter Creek, close to the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, warriors attacked another group of tourists from Helena. A man named Charles Kenck was killed. Another, Jack Stewart, was wounded and robbed. A third, Ben Stone, survived by hiding in the creek for about three hours.
They kept going north for more than three weeks. By the end, they had traveled about eleven hundred and seventy miles.
The siege lasted five days, in freezing cold. Poker Joe was killed. So was Joseph's brother, [Ollokot](/ˈɑləkɑt/). So was Looking Glass, shot when he stepped up onto a bluff, out of cover.

The survivors were not allowed to go home. Four hundred and thirty-two of them were sent first to Fort Leavenworth, in Kansas, then to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma, where many of the newborns and elders died. Only in eighteen eighty-five were they allowed back to the Northwest, and Joseph was never allowed to live in his [Wallowa](/wɑlˈaʊə/) Valley again. He died in nineteen-oh-four on the Colville Reservation in Washington. The Park Service describes him as dying brokenhearted, an exile from his home.
Rebecca Miles, the first woman to chair the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) Tribe, put it simply, looking back on that history: "There's no future without forgiveness."
